items.stem: What is the name for "a leaf with green areas that contain chlorophyll and white areas that do not"?
items.answer: Variegated leaf
items.markingKey: Variegated leaf: a leaf with green areas that contain chlorophyll and white areas that do not.

items.stem: Describe how to test a leaf for starch.
items.answer: Boil the leaf in water to kill it and break membranes; boil in ethanol (hot water bath) to remove chlorophyll; dip in water to soften; add iodine; blue-black shows starch.
items.markingKey: boil in water [1]; ethanol to decolourise [1]; iodine → blue-black [1] [3]

items.stem: A variegated leaf is tested for starch. Explain why only the green parts turn blue-black.
items.answer: Only the green parts contain chlorophyll, which absorbs light for photosynthesis; white parts cannot photosynthesise so do not make starch.
items.markingKey: chlorophyll needed [1]; only green parts make starch [1] [2]

items.stem: Hydrogencarbonate indicator is red at atmospheric CO₂ concentration, yellow at high CO₂ and purple at low CO₂. Tubes were set up and left for 2 hours: tube B with a leaf disc sample, covered in foil (dark); tube C with a leaf disc sample, covered in thin gauze (dim light); tube D with no leaf, in bright light. Predict the colour of the indicator in each tube and explain each prediction.
items.answer: B: yellow — only respiration, CO₂ released; C: red — photosynthesis and respiration about equal (compensation point), no net change; D: red — no living material, so no change (control)
items.markingKey: B: yellow [1], reason [1]; C: red [1], reason [1]; D: red [1], reason [1] [6]

items.stem: Use the balanced equation for photosynthesis, 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂. How many molecules of carbon dioxide are needed to make 10 molecules of glucose, and how many molecules of oxygen are released?
items.answer: 60 CO₂ molecules; 60 O₂ molecules
items.markingKey: ratio 6 CO₂ : 1 glucose : 6 O₂ [1]; 60 and 60 [1] [2]

items.stem: Hydrogencarbonate indicator is red at atmospheric CO₂ concentration, yellow at high CO₂ and purple at low CO₂. Tubes were set up and left for 2 hours: tube A with a leaf disc sample, in bright light; tube B with a leaf disc sample, covered in foil (dark); tube C with a leaf disc sample, covered in thin gauze (dim light); tube D with no leaf, in bright light. Predict the colour of the indicator in each tube and explain each prediction. State the purpose of the tube with no living material, if included.
items.answer: A: purple — photosynthesis faster than respiration, CO₂ taken in; B: yellow — only respiration, CO₂ released; C: red — photosynthesis and respiration about equal (compensation point), no net change; D: red — no living material, so no change (control); the tube without a plant is a control, showing that light alone does not change the indicator.
items.markingKey: A: purple [1], reason [1]; B: yellow [1], reason [1]; C: red [1], reason [1]; D: red [1], reason [1] [8]

items.stem: Noah destarches a potted plant, then leaves a leaf enclosed in a flask containing soda lime (absorbs CO₂) in light for 6 hours before testing it for starch. Result: the leaf stays orange-brown. (a) Explain why the plant was destarched first. (b) Describe how the plant was destarched. (c) State why ethanol must be heated in a water bath, not with a flame.
items.answer: (a) To remove starch already present, so any starch found was made during the experiment. (b) It was kept in the dark for about 48 hours. (c) Ethanol is flammable.
items.markingKey: (a) removes starch [1]; fair test / starch must come from photosynthesis in experiment [1] [2] (b) [1] (c) [1]

items.stem: Ethan destarches a potted plant, then leaves a variegated leaf in light for 6 hours before testing it for starch. Result: only the green areas turn blue-black. (a) Describe how the plant was destarched. (b) Describe how the leaf is tested for starch. (c) State the conclusion of this investigation.
items.answer: (a) It was kept in the dark for about 48 hours. (b) Boil in water, then in ethanol in a hot water bath, rinse, add iodine solution. (c) Chlorophyll is needed for photosynthesis.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) water [1]; ethanol [1]; iodine [1] [3] (c) [1]

items.stem: Which is the balanced equation for photosynthesis?
items.answer: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂
items.markingKey: Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen, in light with chlorophyll.

items.stem: Explain why the leaf is placed in boiling water and then in hot ethanol in the starch test.
items.answer: Boiling water kills the cells and breaks down membranes so iodine can enter; ethanol dissolves chlorophyll so the colour change can be seen.
items.markingKey: membranes broken [1]; chlorophyll removed so colour visible [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why plants convert glucose to starch for storage.
items.answer: Starch is insoluble, so it does not affect the water potential of cells, and it is compact; it can be converted back to glucose when needed.
items.markingKey: insoluble [1]; no effect on osmosis [1] [2]

items.stem: Use the balanced equation for photosynthesis, 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂. How many molecules of carbon dioxide are needed to make 3 molecules of glucose, and how many molecules of oxygen are released?
items.answer: 18 CO₂ molecules; 18 O₂ molecules
items.markingKey: ratio 6 CO₂ : 1 glucose : 6 O₂ [1]; 18 and 18 [1] [2]

items.stem: Use the balanced equation for photosynthesis, 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂. How many molecules of carbon dioxide are needed to make 4 molecules of glucose, and how many molecules of oxygen are released?
items.answer: 24 CO₂ molecules; 24 O₂ molecules
items.markingKey: ratio 6 CO₂ : 1 glucose : 6 O₂ [1]; 24 and 24 [1] [2]

items.stem: Use the balanced equation for photosynthesis, 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂. How many molecules of carbon dioxide are needed to make 5 molecules of glucose, and how many molecules of oxygen are released?
items.answer: 30 CO₂ molecules; 30 O₂ molecules
items.markingKey: ratio 6 CO₂ : 1 glucose : 6 O₂ [1]; 30 and 30 [1] [2]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "limiting factor"?
options: Something present in the environment in such short supply that it restricts life processes.
The amount of light energy reaching a given area; it decreases as the distance from the lamp increases.
The amount of product made (e.g. oxygen) or reactant used per unit time.
The light intensity at which the rate of photosynthesis equals the rate of respiration.
items.answer: Something present in the environment in such short supply that it restricts life processes.
items.markingKey: Limiting factor: something present in the environment in such short supply that it restricts life processes.

items.stem: Explain why the rate of photosynthesis stops increasing at high light intensity.
items.answer: Another factor, such as carbon dioxide concentration or temperature, becomes limiting, so extra light has no effect.
items.markingKey: another factor limiting [1]; named example [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why increasing temperature above about 40 °C decreases the rate of photosynthesis.
items.answer: The enzymes that catalyse photosynthesis become denatured; their active sites change shape.
items.markingKey: enzymes [1]; denatured [1] [2]

items.stem: Hana placed a piece of pondweed in a beaker of dilute sodium hydrogencarbonate solution and counted the bubbles of gas released in one minute with a lamp at different distances. Results table. Distance of lamp from pondweed / cm: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30. Number of bubbles per minute / bubbles/min, trial 1: 55, 45, 37, 31, 23, 18; trial 2: 53, 44, 37, 30, 22, 17; trial 3: 52, 45, 37, 42, 24, 19. Name the gas in the bubbles and describe a test to confirm it.
items.answer: Oxygen: it relights a glowing splint.
items.markingKey: oxygen [1]; relights glowing splint [1] [2]

items.stem: Ana placed a piece of pondweed in a beaker of dilute sodium hydrogencarbonate solution and counted the bubbles of gas released in one minute with a lamp at different distances. Results table. Distance of lamp from pondweed / cm: 10, 15, 20, 30, 40. Number of bubbles per minute / bubbles/min, trial 1: 48, 35, 28, 17, 12; trial 2: 48, 37, 16, 17, 11; trial 3: 45, 39, 30, 17, 12. (a) Suggest one way to improve this investigation. (b) State the type of graph you would draw to display these results and what you would plot on each axis.
items.answer: (a) Measure the volume of gas with a gas syringe instead of counting bubbles. (b) A line graph: distance of lamp from pondweed on the x-axis and mean number of bubbles per minute on the y-axis.
items.markingKey: (a) Any one from: measure the volume of gas with a gas syringe instead of counting bubbles; place a heat shield (beaker of water) between lamp and plant; carry out the experiment in a dark room; repeat each test more times and calculate a mean (to improve reliability); test more values of the distance of lamp from pondweed (smaller intervals), especially near the turning point / extremes [1] (b) line graph (continuous independent variable) [1]; distance of lamp from pondweed on x-axis and number of bubbles per minute on y-axis [1] [2]

items.stem: Aisha placed a piece of pondweed in a beaker of dilute sodium hydrogencarbonate solution and counted the bubbles of gas released in one minute with a lamp at different distances. Results table. Distance of lamp from pondweed / cm: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50. Number of bubbles per minute / bubbles/min, trial 1: 54, 47, 20, 13, 10; trial 2: 53, 32, 20, 13, 9; trial 3: 53, 31, 20, 12, 10. (a) State two variables that should be kept constant in this investigation. (b) Name the gas in the bubbles and describe a test to confirm it.
items.answer: (a) Temperature of the water; concentration of sodium hydrogencarbonate (CO₂). (b) Oxygen: it relights a glowing splint.
items.markingKey: (a) Any two from: temperature of the water; concentration of sodium hydrogencarbonate (CO₂); same piece / mass of pondweed; time allowed to adjust before counting; type of lamp / no other light [2] (b) oxygen [1]; relights glowing splint [1] [2]

items.stem: Kwame placed a piece of pondweed in a beaker of dilute sodium hydrogencarbonate solution and counted the bubbles of gas released in one minute with a lamp at different distances. Results table. Distance of lamp from pondweed / cm: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50. Number of bubbles per minute / bubbles/min, trial 1: 50, 31, 19, 13, 10; trial 2: 51, 30, 20, 19, 9; trial 3: 51, 33, 19, 13, 9. (a) Identify the anomalous result in the table and state what should be done with it. (b) Describe the trend shown by the results.
items.answer: (a) Trial 2 at 40 cm (19 bubbles/min); it should be ignored when calculating the mean (or repeated). (b) As the distance from the lamp increases, the number of bubbles per minute decreases (light intensity falls).
items.markingKey: (a) trial 2 at 40 cm identified [1]; ignore / repeat it [1] [2] (b) correct overall pattern [1]; data quoted with units / turning point given [1] [2]

items.stem: Amara placed a piece of pondweed in a beaker of dilute sodium hydrogencarbonate solution and counted the bubbles of gas released in one minute with a lamp at different distances. Results table. Distance of lamp from pondweed / cm: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30. Number of bubbles per minute / bubbles/min, trial 1: 57, 52, 39, 32, 25, 19; trial 2: 57, 48, 58, 33, 26, 19; trial 3: 62, 48, 42, 31, 25, 20. (a) Explain the results. (b) Calculate the relative light intensity at 5 cm and at 10 cm, using light intensity = 1 ÷ distance².
items.answer: (a) Closer to the lamp the light intensity is higher (∝ 1/d²), so more light energy is absorbed by chlorophyll and the rate of photosynthesis, and oxygen production, is greater. At the shortest distances another factor such as CO₂ or temperature may limit the rate. (b) 4.00 × 10⁻² and 1.00 × 10⁻² (arbitrary units)
items.markingKey: (a) light intensity greater when closer [1]; more photosynthesis / oxygen [1]; limiting factor at short distance [1] [3] (b) 1 ÷ 5² = 4.00 × 10⁻² [1]; 1 ÷ 10² = 1.00 × 10⁻² [1] [2]

items.stem: At low light intensity, which factor limits the rate of photosynthesis?
items.answer: Light intensity
items.markingKey: Increasing the limiting factor increases the rate.

items.stem: Explain why counting bubbles is not an accurate way to measure the rate of photosynthesis of pondweed.
items.answer: Bubbles may be different sizes and some gas may dissolve in water; measuring the volume of gas in a gas syringe or capillary tube is more accurate.
items.markingKey: bubble size varies [1]; better method [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the rate of photosynthesis is higher on a warm sunny day than on a cold sunny day, even though light intensity is the same.
items.answer: Photosynthesis is controlled by enzymes; at higher temperatures molecules have more kinetic energy and collide more often, so temperature was limiting on the cold day.
items.markingKey: temperature limiting [1]; enzymes / kinetic energy [1] [2]

items.stem: A lamp is moved further from a plant, from 15 cm to 45 cm. Using light intensity ∝ 1 ÷ distance², calculate the factor by which the light intensity changes.
items.markingKey: ratio of distances 15 ÷ 45 [1]; squared = 0.111 [1] [2]

items.stem: A tomato grower in Hanoi increases the carbon dioxide concentration in a greenhouse from 0.03% to 0.12% and the yield rises from 48 kg to 60 kg per row. (a) Calculate the percentage increase in yield. (b) Explain why increasing carbon dioxide increased the yield.
items.answer: (a) 25% (b) CO₂ was a limiting factor; more CO₂ increases the rate of photosynthesis, so more glucose is made for growth (and fruit).
items.markingKey: (a) (60 − 48) ÷ 48 × 100 [1] = 25% [1] [2] (b) CO₂ limiting [1]; more photosynthesis → more carbohydrate for growth [1] [2]

items.stem: Noah placed equal lengths of pondweed in solutions of sodium hydrogencarbonate of different concentrations, with the lamp at a fixed distance, and measured the volume of oxygen produced in 5 minutes. Results table. Concentration of sodium hydrogencarbonate / %: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2. Volume of oxygen / mm³, trial 1: 4, 31, 47, 67, 78; trial 2: 4, 18, 47, 67, 76; trial 3: 4, 31, 48, 64, 78. (a) Describe the trend shown by the results. (b) Explain the results.
items.answer: (a) As the concentration of sodium hydrogencarbonate increases, the volume of oxygen increases (from 4 to 77.33). (b) Sodium hydrogencarbonate releases carbon dioxide, a raw material of photosynthesis; at low concentrations CO₂ is limiting so more CO₂ increases the rate; at high concentrations another factor (light or temperature) limits the rate, so the curve levels off.
items.markingKey: (a) correct overall pattern [1]; data quoted with units / turning point given [1] [2] (b) CO₂ is a raw material [1]; CO₂ limiting at low concentration [1]; another factor limiting at high concentration [1] [3]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "stomata"?
options: Reduces water loss by evaporation and is transparent to let light through.
Thin and transparent so light passes to the palisade layer.
Pores, mostly in the lower epidermis, that let carbon dioxide in and oxygen and water vapour out.
items.answer: Pores, mostly in the lower epidermis, that let carbon dioxide in and oxygen and water vapour out.
items.markingKey: Stomata: pores, mostly in the lower epidermis, that let carbon dioxide in and oxygen and water vapour out.

items.stem: Explain how the structure of the palisade mesophyll is adapted for photosynthesis.
items.answer: Cells are near the upper surface, tightly packed and column-shaped with many chloroplasts, so they absorb as much light as possible.
items.markingKey: position near top / packed [1]; many chloroplasts [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why most stomata are on the lower surface of a leaf.
items.answer: The lower surface is shaded and cooler, so less water is lost by evaporation, while gases can still diffuse in and out.
items.markingKey: cooler / shaded [1]; less water loss [1] [2]

items.stem: A nail-varnish peel from the lower surface of a hibiscus leaf was viewed with a microscope. The field of view has a diameter of 0.4 mm and contains 33 stomata. Calculate the number of stomata per mm².
items.answer: 263 per mm²

items.stem: Zara counted stomata in five fields of view on the lower surface of a maize leaf. Counts: 21, 57, 20, 35, 45. The field of view has a diameter of 0.4 mm. (a) Calculate the mean number of stomata per field of view. (b) Calculate the stomatal density in stomata per mm².
items.answer: (a) 35.6 (b) 283 per mm²

items.stem: Botanists compare the leaves of a plant growing in a hot, dry desert with those of a plant growing in a garden in Lima. (a) Describe the path taken by a carbon dioxide molecule from the air to a chloroplast in a palisade cell. (b) Name the tissue that carries sucrose away from the leaf.
items.answer: (a) Through a stoma, into the air spaces of the spongy mesophyll, diffuses through the cell wall and membrane of the palisade cell into the chloroplast. (b) Phloem.
items.markingKey: (a) stoma [1]; air spaces [1]; diffuses into cell [1] [3] (b) [1]

items.stem: Explain the importance of air spaces in the spongy mesophyll.
items.answer: They allow carbon dioxide to diffuse from stomata to the mesophyll cells and oxygen to diffuse out; they give a large surface area for gas exchange.
items.markingKey: diffusion of CO₂ / O₂ [1]; large surface for exchange [1] [2]

items.stem: For each part of a leaf, describe how it is adapted for photosynthesis: (i) spongy mesophyll (ii) waxy cuticle (iii) upper epidermis.
items.answer: (i) cells with air spaces between them for diffusion of gases (ii) reduces water loss by evaporation and is transparent to let light through (iii) thin and transparent so light passes to the palisade layer
items.markingKey: (i) cells with air spaces between them for diffusion of gases [1]; (ii) reduces water loss by evaporation and is transparent to let light through [1]; (iii) thin and transparent so light passes to the palisade layer [1] [3]

items.stem: For each part of a leaf, describe how it is adapted for photosynthesis: (i) vascular bundle (ii) spongy mesophyll (iii) waxy cuticle.
items.answer: (i) contains xylem, bringing water and mineral ions, and phloem, carrying sucrose away (ii) cells with air spaces between them for diffusion of gases (iii) reduces water loss by evaporation and is transparent to let light through
items.markingKey: (i) contains xylem, bringing water and mineral ions, and phloem, carrying sucrose away [1]; (ii) cells with air spaces between them for diffusion of gases [1]; (iii) reduces water loss by evaporation and is transparent to let light through [1] [3]

items.stem: Botanists compare the leaves of a plant growing in the surface of a pond (floating leaves) with those of a plant growing in a garden in Cape Town. (a) Describe the path taken by a carbon dioxide molecule from the air to a chloroplast in a palisade cell. (b) Explain why leaves have a large surface area. (c) Name the tissue that carries sucrose away from the leaf.
items.answer: (a) Through a stoma, into the air spaces of the spongy mesophyll, diffuses through the cell wall and membrane of the palisade cell into the chloroplast. (b) To absorb more light and to provide more surface for gas exchange. (c) Phloem.
items.markingKey: (a) stoma [1]; air spaces [1]; diffuses into cell [1] [3] (b) [2] (c) [1]

items.stem: What is the name for "a substance added to soil to supply mineral ions such as nitrate, phosphate and potassium"?
items.answer: Fertiliser
items.markingKey: Fertiliser: a substance added to soil to supply mineral ions such as nitrate, phosphate and potassium.

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "nitrate ions"?
options: Yellowing of leaves caused by a lack of chlorophyll, for example from magnesium deficiency.
Mineral ions needed by plants to make chlorophyll.
Mineral ions needed by plants to make amino acids and proteins.
A substance added to soil to supply mineral ions such as nitrate, phosphate and potassium.
items.answer: Mineral ions needed by plants to make amino acids and proteins.
items.markingKey: Nitrate ions: mineral ions needed by plants to make amino acids and proteins.

items.stem: Explain why a plant lacking magnesium grows slowly.
items.answer: Magnesium is needed for chlorophyll; with less chlorophyll less light is absorbed, so less photosynthesis and less glucose for growth.
items.markingKey: less chlorophyll [1]; less photosynthesis / glucose [1] [2]

items.stem: Jonas grew seedlings in three culture solutions for four weeks. Mean dry mass: complete solution 6.7 g; lacking nitrate 2.1 g; lacking magnesium 3.9 g. (a) Calculate the percentage decrease in dry mass caused by lack of nitrate. (b) Describe the appearance of the leaves of the seedlings lacking magnesium.
items.answer: (a) 68.7% (b) yellow leaves (chlorosis)

items.stem: A farmer in Singapore notices that the maize plants in one field are small with pale yellow leaves. (a) Suggest two mineral deficiencies that could cause these symptoms. (b) Suggest one disadvantage of adding too much fertiliser.
items.answer: (a) Nitrate deficiency and magnesium deficiency. (b) Excess runs off into rivers, causing eutrophication (or it wastes money / damages roots).

items.stem: Explain why a plant lacking nitrate has stunted growth.
items.answer: Nitrate is needed to make amino acids and proteins; without proteins the plant cannot make new cells for growth.
items.markingKey: amino acids / proteins [1]; new cells / growth [1] [2]

items.stem: Mohammed grew seedlings in three culture solutions for four weeks. Mean dry mass: complete solution 5.6 g; lacking nitrate 2.1 g; lacking magnesium 3.8 g. (a) Calculate the percentage decrease in dry mass caused by lack of nitrate. (b) Describe the appearance of the leaves of the seedlings lacking magnesium. (c) Explain why lack of nitrate reduced growth.
items.answer: (a) 62.5% (b) yellow leaves (chlorosis) (c) Nitrate is needed to make amino acids and proteins for new cells.
items.markingKey: (a) (5.6 − 2.1) ÷ 5.6 × 100 [1] = 62.5% [1] (b) yellow / chlorosis [1] (c) amino acids / proteins [1]; growth / new cells [1] [5]

items.stem: What is the role of chlorophyll in photosynthesis?
options: It transports water to the leaf
It absorbs carbon dioxide from the air
It transfers light energy into chemical energy
items.answer: It transfers light energy into chemical energy
items.markingKey: Chlorophyll absorbs light; the energy is used to make carbohydrates.

items.stem: Explain why a leaf kept in a flask containing sodium hydroxide (which absorbs CO₂) does not make starch.
items.answer: Carbon dioxide is a raw material for photosynthesis; without it no glucose and therefore no starch can be made.
items.markingKey: CO₂ absorbed / not available [1]; needed to make glucose [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why hydrogencarbonate indicator around a water plant turns purple in bright light.
items.answer: In bright light the rate of photosynthesis is greater than respiration, so the plant takes in carbon dioxide; less CO₂ makes the indicator purple.
items.markingKey: photosynthesis > respiration [1]; CO₂ removed [1] [2]

items.stem: Hydrogencarbonate indicator is red at atmospheric CO₂ concentration, yellow at high CO₂ and purple at low CO₂. Tubes were set up and left for 2 hours: tube A with a piece of pondweed, in bright light; tube B with a piece of pondweed, covered in foil (dark); tube D with no leaf, in bright light. Predict the colour of the indicator in each tube and explain each prediction.
items.answer: A: purple — photosynthesis faster than respiration, CO₂ taken in; B: yellow — only respiration, CO₂ released; D: red — no living material, so no change (control)
items.markingKey: A: purple [1], reason [1]; B: yellow [1], reason [1]; D: red [1], reason [1] [6]

items.stem: Hydrogencarbonate indicator is red at atmospheric CO₂ concentration, yellow at high CO₂ and purple at low CO₂. Tubes were set up and left for 2 hours: tube A with a leaf, in bright light; tube B with a leaf, covered in foil (dark); tube C with a leaf, covered in thin gauze (dim light). Predict the colour of the indicator in each tube and explain each prediction.
items.answer: A: purple — photosynthesis faster than respiration, CO₂ taken in; B: yellow — only respiration, CO₂ released; C: red — photosynthesis and respiration about equal (compensation point), no net change
items.markingKey: A: purple [1], reason [1]; B: yellow [1], reason [1]; C: red [1], reason [1] [6]

items.stem: Describe how a plant makes and uses the glucose produced in photosynthesis.
items.answer: Chlorophyll in chloroplasts absorbs light; energy used to combine CO₂ (from air via stomata) and water (from roots via xylem) to make glucose, releasing oxygen. Glucose used for respiration, stored as starch, made into cellulose, sucrose for transport, amino acids with nitrate ions, fats and oils.
items.markingKey: raw materials and source [1]; chlorophyll / light [1]; products [1]; three uses [3] [6]

items.stem: A lamp is moved from 20 cm to 10 cm from a plant. By what factor does the light intensity increase?
items.markingKey: Light intensity ∝ 1/distance²: halving the distance gives 2² = 4 times the intensity.

items.stem: Explain why a greenhouse owner might not increase carbon dioxide above a certain concentration.
items.answer: Above that level another factor (light or temperature) limits the rate, so the extra CO₂ gives no extra yield and costs money.
items.markingKey: another factor limiting [1]; cost vs benefit [1] [2]

items.stem: A student in Lagos states: "Doubling the distance of the lamp halves the light intensity." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Light intensity is proportional to 1/distance², so doubling the distance reduces it to a quarter.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Light intensity is proportional to 1/distance², so doubling the distance reduces it to a quarter. [2]

Number of bubbles per minute / bubbles/min, trial 1: 66, 51, 43, 33, 26, 20; trial 2: 65, 57, 26, 33, 25, 22; trial 3: 62, 55, 41, 35, 25, 20. items.markingKey: line graph (continuous independent variable) [1]; distance of lamp from pondweed on x-axis and number of bubbles per minute on y-axis [1] [2]

items.answer: (a) As the concentration of sodium hydrogencarbonate increases, the volume of oxygen increases (from 4 to 77.33). (b) Use a water bath to keep the temperature constant.

items.stem: A tomato grower in Lima increases the carbon dioxide concentration in a greenhouse from 0.03% to 0.12% and the yield rises from 40 kg to 53 kg per row. (a) Calculate the percentage increase in yield. (b) Evaluate whether the grower should increase carbon dioxide concentration even further.
items.answer: (a) 32.5% (b) Not necessarily: above a certain concentration another factor limits the rate, so yield would not increase; the cost of extra CO₂ may exceed extra income; very high CO₂ can harm workers.
items.markingKey: (a) (53 − 40) ÷ 40 × 100 [1] = 32.5% [1] [2] (b) another factor limiting [1]; cost / economic argument [1]; conclusion [1] [3]

items.stem: Which term is defined as "tightly packed cells with many chloroplasts near the upper surface, absorbing most light"?
items.answer: Palisade mesophyll
items.markingKey: Palisade mesophyll: tightly packed cells with many chloroplasts near the upper surface, absorbing most light.

items.stem: Explain why the upper epidermis has no chloroplasts.
items.answer: It is transparent so that light passes through to the palisade cells below where most photosynthesis happens.
items.markingKey: transparent [1]; light reaches palisade [1] [2]

items.stem: A nail-varnish peel from the lower surface of a pea leaf was viewed with a microscope. The field of view has a diameter of 0.5 mm and contains 40 stomata. Calculate the number of stomata per mm².
items.answer: 204 per mm²

items.stem: Describe how the internal structure of a leaf is adapted for photosynthesis.
items.answer: Transparent cuticle and epidermis let light in; palisade near top with many chloroplasts; spongy mesophyll with air spaces for diffusion; stomata for gas exchange with guard cells; xylem brings water, phloem removes sugars; thin for short diffusion distance.
items.markingKey: any five adaptations linked to function [5]

items.stem: Botanists compare the leaves of a plant growing in the surface of a pond (floating leaves) with those of a plant growing in a garden in Accra. (a) Suggest how the leaves of the plant from this habitat may differ, and explain why. (b) Explain why leaves have a large surface area. (c) Explain how guard cells control the opening of stomata.
items.answer: (a) Stomata on the upper surface only, because the lower surface is in water. (b) To absorb more light and to provide more surface for gas exchange. (c) When guard cells take in water by osmosis they become turgid and curve apart, opening the stoma; when they lose water they become flaccid and close it.
items.markingKey: (a) difference [1]; explanation linked to habitat [1] [2] (b) [2] (c) turgid → open [1]; flaccid → close [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why farmers add fertilisers to fields where crops are harvested each year.
items.answer: Harvesting removes the plants and the mineral ions they absorbed, so the soil runs short; fertilisers replace the ions to keep yields high.
items.markingKey: ions removed with crop [1]; replaced [1] [2]

items.stem: Daniel grew seedlings in three culture solutions for four weeks. Mean dry mass: complete solution 6.4 g; lacking nitrate 3.1 g; lacking magnesium 4.4 g. (a) Calculate the percentage decrease in dry mass caused by lack of nitrate. (b) Describe the appearance of the leaves of the seedlings lacking magnesium.
items.answer: (a) 51.6% (b) yellow leaves (chlorosis)

items.stem: Felix grew seedlings in three culture solutions for four weeks. Mean dry mass: complete solution 6.7 g; lacking nitrate 2.6 g; lacking magnesium 4.8 g. items.answer: So that any starch found must have been made during the experiment

items.stem: A student in Jakarta states: "Photosynthesis produces carbon dioxide." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and produces glucose and oxygen.

items.stem: A student in Colombo states: "Plants get their food from the soil through their roots." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Plants make their own carbohydrates by photosynthesis; the soil provides water and mineral ions only.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Plants make their own carbohydrates by photosynthesis; the soil provides water and mineral ions only. [2]

items.stem: Hydrogencarbonate indicator is red at atmospheric CO₂ concentration, yellow at high CO₂ and purple at low CO₂. Tubes were set up and left for 2 hours: tube A with a leaf disc sample, in bright light; tube C with a leaf disc sample, covered in thin gauze (dim light); tube D with no leaf, in bright light. Predict the colour of the indicator in each tube and explain each prediction.
items.answer: A: purple — photosynthesis faster than respiration, CO₂ taken in; C: red — photosynthesis and respiration about equal (compensation point), no net change; D: red — no living material, so no change (control)
items.markingKey: A: purple [1], reason [1]; C: red [1], reason [1]; D: red [1], reason [1] [6]

items.stem: Hydrogencarbonate indicator is red at atmospheric CO₂ concentration, yellow at high CO₂ and purple at low CO₂. Predict the colour of the indicator in each tube and explain each prediction.
items.answer: A: purple — photosynthesis faster than respiration, CO₂ taken in; B: yellow — only respiration, CO₂ released; C: red — photosynthesis and respiration about equal (compensation point), no net change
items.markingKey: A: purple [1], reason [1]; B: yellow [1], reason [1]; C: red [1], reason [1] [6]

items.stem: Tomás destarches a potted plant, then leaves a leaf partly covered with a strip of black paper in light for 6 hours before testing it for starch. Result: the covered strip stays orange-brown; the rest turns blue-black. (a) Explain why the plant was destarched first. (b) Describe how the plant was destarched. (c) Describe how the leaf is tested for starch.
items.answer: (a) To remove starch already present, so any starch found was made during the experiment. (b) It was kept in the dark for about 48 hours. (c) Boil in water, then in ethanol in a hot water bath, rinse, add iodine solution.
items.markingKey: (a) removes starch [1]; fair test / starch must come from photosynthesis in experiment [1] [2] (b) [1] (c) water [1]; ethanol [1]; iodine [1] [3]

items.stem: Mohammed says: "The higher the temperature, the faster the rate of photosynthesis, at any temperature." Explain whether Mohammed is correct.
items.answer: Above the optimum, enzymes are denatured and the rate falls.

items.stem: A lamp is moved further from a plant, from 15 cm to 30 cm. Using light intensity ∝ 1 ÷ distance², calculate the factor by which the light intensity changes. Predict the effect on the rate of photosynthesis, assuming light is the limiting factor.
items.answer: ×0.25; rate decreases (but not necessarily by the same factor).

items.stem: Describe and explain how a grower could use a greenhouse to increase crop yield, referring to limiting factors.
items.answer: Artificial lighting increases light intensity / hours; heaters keep the temperature near the optimum for enzymes; burning paraffin or adding CO₂ increases CO₂; each removes a limiting factor so the rate of photosynthesis and growth increases; balance cost against extra yield.
items.markingKey: light [1]; temperature [1]; CO₂ [1]; limiting factor idea [1]; cost-benefit [1] [5]

items.stem: State the function of guard cells.
items.answer: To open and close the stomata, controlling gas exchange and water loss.

items.stem: Explain how the vascular bundles support photosynthesis in the leaf.
items.answer: Xylem brings water (a raw material) and mineral ions; phloem carries away sucrose made from glucose so it does not build up.
items.markingKey: xylem brings water [1]; phloem removes sugars [1] [2]

items.stem: A nail-varnish peel from the lower surface of a privet leaf was viewed with a microscope. The field of view has a diameter of 1 mm and contains 42 stomata. Calculate the number of stomata per mm².
items.answer: 53 per mm²

items.stem: Botanists compare the leaves of a plant growing in a hot, dry desert with those of a plant growing in a garden in Colombo. (a) Describe the path taken by a carbon dioxide molecule from the air to a chloroplast in a palisade cell. (b) Explain why leaves have a large surface area.
items.answer: (a) Through a stoma, into the air spaces of the spongy mesophyll, diffuses through the cell wall and membrane of the palisade cell into the chloroplast. (b) To absorb more light and to provide more surface for gas exchange.
